summary: This RFC documents updates to the Domain Name System specifications RFC 882 and RFC 883, suggests operational guidelines, and discusses experience and problems. It was replaced by RFC 1034 and RFC 1035.

plainLanguage.summary: The people running the new naming system shared what they learned and what to change in the first rules.

questions: what changed in the early domain name system
subtitle: Updates and lessons learned from early DNS implementation.

tldr.problem: The initial Domain Name System specifications needed refinements based on early implementation experience and operational constraints.
tldr.mechanism: Gathers changes and clarifications to DNS specifications, operational guidelines, and documents known issues and shortcomings discovered in practice.
tldr.outcome: RFC 973 has been replaced by RFCs 1034 and 1035, which provide consolidated DNS specifications.

today: RFC 973 has been replaced by RFC 1034 and RFC 1035, which provide consolidated and more complete Domain Name System specifications that supersede both RFC 882/883 and RFC 973.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: RFC 973 documents changes to the Domain Name System specifications (RFC 882 and RFC 883) that are in widespread use and should be regarded as part of the specification. It also provides operational guidelines for configuring DNS databases, discusses unusual situations and common bugs encountered in practice, and identifies shortcomings that may be addressed in future versions.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo shares what people learned from running the first domain name system and what should change in the rules.

sections.title: Key Updates to the Specification
sections.content:
Several important changes are documented as final updates that should be incorporated in all DNS software:

TTL field expansion: The original TTL field used a 16 bit representation that could show a maximum of about 18 hours. All time values, including TTLs and the MINIMUM field of the SOA record, were expanded to 32 bits.

Resource record types: Class 2 (originally for CSNET) is now obsolete, and Class 3 has been assigned for CHAOS. The MD and MF record types for mail agent binding are replaced by a new MX (Mail Exchange) record type, which conveys mail routing information in a single record type rather than two separate types.

CNAME handling: If a node has a CNAME (Canonical Name) record, it should have no other records at that node to avoid ambiguity between alias and primary names.

Wildcard semantics: The use of the wildcard label (represented as an asterisk) is refined. A single wildcard label in the leftmost part of a zone can match any number of unknown labels or a single known label, but only for parts of the tree that are neither delegated nor explicitly represented.

Zone transfer ordering: Zone transfers may now occur in any order, as long as the SOA record is transmitted first and last with no duplication elsewhere.

Master file format: Domain names in master files are represented as either absolute (ending with a dot) or relative to the current origin.
sections.plainLanguage: The updates included making time fields bigger, simplifying how to tell mail where to go, being clearer about what wildcards mean, and making master file format simpler.

sections.title: Operational Guidelines
sections.content:
The RFC provides practical guidelines for DNS zone delegation and configuration:

Zone delegation synchronization: When a domain becomes independent, the delegation records in both parent and child zones should be carefully synchronized. The NS records, A records for nameservers, and TTLs should all be identical to ensure consistent resolution regardless of which server is queried.

SOA serial numbers: The serial field in the SOA record should be continuously incremented (modulo 2^32) and incremented each time the zone is modified to enable change detection via secondary servers.

TTL consistency: All resource records with the same name, class, and type should have the same TTL so that cached records timeout simultaneously.

Case handling and aliases: Domain names should be case-consistent in the database (case-insensitive resolution, but consistent representation). Canonical names should be preferred to aliases in all record types to ensure uniqueness and reliable comparisons.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep parent and child zone records in sync, increment version numbers when you make changes, make sure records expire together, and prefer real names over nicknames.

sections.title: Experiences and Problem Areas
sections.content:
Common issues in practice: UDP checksums were generated incorrectly in many UNIX implementations, causing failures when communicating with non-UNIX systems. Some servers returned incorrect records for root servers or made up data with artificially high TTLs, which then persisted in caches. The RFC emphasizes: "If you must lie, lie only to yourself" (about other parts of the name space).

Open problems: The present system has shortcomings in caching negative results (names that do not exist), which make up a larger than expected percentage of queries. The specification lacks a standard method for caching non-existent names. Additionally, name compression in messages conflicts with the desire to cache records of types the receiver does not understand. Cache conflicts also arise when a resolver receives replies containing records already in its cache with different TTLs.
sections.plainLanguage: Some implementations had bugs, and people sometimes put fake records in their caches that never went away. The system also doesn't handle 'this name does not exist' answers well.
